fixes.explanation: Right in the first verse: "You restored Jacob from captivity." Here Jacob stands for God's people. The sons of Korah, who wrote this song, open by remembering what the LORD already did. Good news like that is worth telling twice.

That's it, friend: "You forgave the iniquity of Your people…" Iniquity is a heavy word, and the verse puts forgiveness right beside it. The singers put it right in the song. Then comes the word Selah, which I take as a spot to pause and let it sink in.

That's the word. "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" The revival has a purpose in the song: rejoicing in Him. I think a revived people with nothing to rejoice about would be like a fresh batch with no chocolate chips, and nobody wants that batch.

Settling down sounds peaceful, baker, but it's not the word here. The verse asks, "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" Rejoice is a bigger word than settle. They're asking to be brought back to life so they can celebrate Him.

Yes, baker. He says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say…" He did all that asking, and now he says he will listen. A lot of us ask and then start talking again before anybody answers. This singer says he's going to listen.
The singer doesn't mention a scroll in this verse, friend. He says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say…" The song keeps it simple. After all the asking, he says he will listen.

The singer says the opposite, friend. Verse 9 says, "Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him…" Near means close, and the singer opens with surely, so he isn't hedging. I'd say that's a man who has already made up his mind about how close God is.

No sea in this verse, friend. The singer says, "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven." The two places he names are earth and heaven. The sea never makes the list.

Mountains are a fine guess, baker, but the singer picked other spots. He says, "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven." One comes up and one looks down. That's a whole picture, and it didn't need a single mountain.

Yes, baker: "The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase." Indeed is the singer planting his flag. He isn't saying the LORD might provide good. He's saying it will happen, and I'd put that on a cookie box.

No wall in this verse, baker. It says, "The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase." The singer is looking at what the LORD provides and what the land yields. A wall is a fine thing, but it didn't make this batch.
